planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in fall or early spring into consistently moist, humus-rich woodland soil in deep shade; the rhizomatous clumps establish slowly and spread over several seasons once rooted in cool, duff-covered soil.

directions: Pathfinder forms a loose rosette of broad, arrow-shaped leaves that are plain green above but densely white-woolly beneath, so a single brushing hand or footstep flips a leaf and leaves a visible pale trail across the forest floor. Plant divisions into deep, humus-rich duff in full shade beneath established tree canopy, where the thin rhizomes can creep slowly outward through consistently cool, moist soil. Tall, sparsely branched flowering stalks rise above the foliage in summer bearing small greenish-white flowers that mature into tiny sticky, glandular burs dispersed on animal fur. Established colonies need little care beyond a leaf-litter mulch and reliable summer moisture, since the species comes from redwood and Douglas-fir forest floors that rarely dry out.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System — Adenocaulon bicolor

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into well-drained, duff-covered soil beneath redwood, tanoak, or oak canopy; water regularly through the first dry season to establish roots.

directions: Round-fruited sedge forms neat, arching tufts of narrow blue-green blades that stay evergreen through the dry Northern California summer, making it one of the few clumping sedges that genuinely tolerates dry shade beneath redwood and tanoak canopy. Plant divisions or container stock in spring into well-drained duff-covered soil, watering regularly the first season to establish roots before relying on natural rainfall. Inconspicuous brownish flower spikes appear on short stalks in late spring, followed by the small globose fruiting heads that give the species its name. Once established, clumps need no summer irrigation and slowly thicken rather than spread aggressively, making this sedge useful as an unobtrusive filler beneath native shade trees.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich soil beneath redwood or Douglas-fir canopy, keeping the root zone consistently damp through the first growing season.

directions: Pacific woodrush grows in tidy, grass-like tufts of flat, hairy-edged blades that stay green through winter beneath redwood and Douglas-fir canopy where little light reaches the forest floor. Plant divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich soil and keep the root zone consistently damp through the first growing season while the fibrous roots knit together. Small clusters of brown, chestnut-tinged flowers appear on short stalks in spring, followed by seed capsules that allow the clumps to self-sow modestly in favorable duff. Once established, this woodrush tolerates deep shade and competition from tree roots better than most true grasses, making it a useful fine-textured filler at the base of shade trees.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery plugs in fall into moist, duff-rich soil beneath redwood or mixed evergreen canopy so winter rains settle the roots before spring flowering.

directions: Two-eyed violet produces low rosettes of heart-shaped leaves and distinctive white flowers marked with fine purple veins and a pair of small orange-yellow blotches at the throat, giving each bloom its 'two-eyed' appearance. Plant divisions or nursery plugs in fall into moist, duff-rich soil beneath redwood or mixed evergreen forest canopy, where winter rains will settle the roots in before spring flowering. Established clumps die back to a dormant rootstock during the dry summer months typical of the fog belt and rebound with fresh growth once fall rains return. Keep plantings in consistent shade and avoid summer irrigation extremes, mimicking the natural wet-winter, dry-summer rhythm of its coastal forest habitat.

planting.note: Plant in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade at a redwood forest edge or beneath open understory shrubs, watering regularly the first year to establish the root crown.

directions: Seaside alumroot forms a dense mound of rounded, deeply lobed leaves covered in soft, shaggy hairs that help the foliage cope with salt-laden coastal fog along the redwood belt's forest edges and bluffs. Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, siting it where morning sun gives way to afternoon shade beneath taller trees or shrubs. Thin, wiry flower stalks rise above the foliage in late spring carrying small, bell-shaped greenish-white to pink flowers that draw hummingbirds and native bees. Water regularly during the first year to establish the root crown, then rely mainly on coastal fog and winter rain, dividing congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs in fall at the edge of redwood or mixed evergreen forest canopy, in humus-rich but sharply draining soil that stays on the dry side through summer dormancy.

directions: Redwood lily grows along the dry, sunlit edges and open gaps within redwood and mixed evergreen forest, sending up a slender, lightly leafy stem topped by a handful of nodding, bell-shaped flowers that open pale pink to near-white and deepen to a dusky wine-red with maturity, giving rise to its alternate name, chaparral lily. Plant dormant bulbs in fall at the edge of tree canopy, in humus-rich but sharply draining soil that stays on the dry side through summer dormancy, since the bulbs are prone to rot in soil that remains wet after bloom. Give plants dappled morning light or partial shade rather than deep shade, mimicking the filtered light of a forest clearing where the species naturally flowers in early to mid summer. Avoid disturbing the bulbs once established, as this lily resents transplanting and may take a season or two to resume vigorous bloom afterward.
